As Blanche hits the campaign trail, new DOJ memo relaxes rules around political conduct for Senate-approved appointees
Politics
Updated on Oct 9, 2026 5:52 PM EDT — Published on
Oct 9, 2026 2:53 PM EDT
The Department of Justice is making it easier for Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Senate-confirmed DOJ appointees to participate in political activities, according to a new internal memo obtained by PBS News.
The memo, penned by the agency's top ethics official, includes new language noting that Senate-approved presidential appointees are exempt from strict restrictions that govern the political conduct of most senior officials. It specifically allows those employees, including the attorney general, to address political gatherings and endorse or oppose candidates – a swerve away from long-standing precedent within the DOJ that experts say may further erode trust in the U.S. justice system.
WATCH: How Blanche is shattering DOJ's standard of political independence
The document is the latest version of a memo the department's ethics office circulates from time to time, reminding employees of the restrictions on their political activities under a law known as the Hatch Act.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
The existence of exceptions for presidential Senate-confirmed appointees themselves is not new, and is codified in the language of the Hatch Act, which governs the political activity of all federal employees. But presidential appointees at the Department of Justice have a history of holding themselves to a more restrictive code of conduct, noted Joseph Tirrell, who led the DOJ's Departmental Ethics Office before his dismissal last year.
"This policy, and its recent update, have lowered the bar so that DOJ employees are now only held to the standard set by [the Hatch Act], as opposed to the higher and more restrictive standard set by attorneys general for the last 20-plus years that help ensure, to the greatest extent possible, that DOJ was above politicking," Tirrell wrote in an email to PBS News. "DOJ's lowering of its standards regarding political activism by senior officials means that Americans can no longer trust that Department decisions and actions are made fairly and without regard to political affiliation."
The updated guidance comes as Blanche has made a number of appearances at political rallies and official events where political candidates spoke. Recent events have included an election rally for a Senate candidate in North Carolina, where Blanche introduced President Donald Trump, the Republican Party's midterm election convention, as well as a roundtable on violent crime in South Carolina, where Blanche sat next to Sen. Darline Graham, who is on the ballot in November.
READ MORE: Attorney General Blanche blurs Justice Department boundaries by appearing at political events
Tirrell said he believes these appearances still violate a separate Hatch Act prohibition on the use of official authority to influence the outcome of elections.
Previous iterations of the same DOJ document said some individuals serving in "further restricted" positions, like those in the Senior Executive Service (SES), were barred from an even wider array of election activities – including addressing a political rally or endorsing a political candidate – than most other career executive branch employees.
The latest revision lists most of the same "further restricted" roles, but adds a new line specifically exempting "employees appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate (PAS)." And in a section listing the prohibited activities for "further restricted employees," the memo explicitly states that it does not apply to "PAS."
That acronym for presidential appointees is common in other contexts, but recent previous versions of the same DOJ ethics guidance make no such distinctions between those appointees and other "further restricted" employees.
In a statement to PBS, a Department of Justice spokesperson said that the updated version of the memo clarifies, rather than changes, Hatch Act rules.
"The updated guidance clarifies an existing exception under the Hatch Act for Presidentially-appointed, Senate-confirmed officials, and clarifies that appearances with partisan candidates should be reviewed by ethics officials to ensure proper designations," the spokesperson said.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche waves as he arrives on stage at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026. Photo by Brian Snyder/ Reuters
The new language clarifying rules for employees' official appearances with partisan candidates no longer recommends employees avoid appearing alongside political candidates at official events taking place shortly before a political election.
The previous guidance, released when Blanche's predecessor Pam Bondi was serving in the top role, said:
"Previous Attorneys General have made an effort, and also encouraged Presidentially appointed officials, or those acting in such positions, to avoid making public appearances in any state shortly before a primary or general election in that state, to the greatest extent practicable. The Attorney General has determined that this precedent should be followed."

Nation
Updated on Oct 9, 2026 6:20 PM EDT — Published on
Oct 7, 2026 9:20 AM EDT
GULF BREEZE, Fla. (AP) — Intensifying winds whipped palm trees along the beaches of the Florida Panhandle and Alabama on Friday as Hurricane Isaias swirled just offshore, charging toward the U.S. Gulf Coast.
Track the path of Tropical Storm Isaias below.
The Category 3 storm weakened only slightly in the afternoon and was on course to arrive in the evening as a major hurricane — and the first hurricane of an unusually quiet Atlantic season.
READ MORE: How El Niño is playing a role in Hurricane Isaias
Tracking late Friday afternoon showed landfall would likely take place over the western panhandle near the Pensacola area, said Robbie Berg, a national warning coordinator for the National Hurricane Center.
Grow your mind
Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the
wide worlds of science, health and technology.
Forecasters warned of a significant storm surge, damaging winds, flooding and possibly even tornadoes before the storm loses steam as it moves inland and delivers strong winds and rain well north into Atlanta.
Tropical storm-force winds began to lash the Gulf shoreline around midday, hours before Isaias was expected to come ashore in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white sand beaches that are dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.
A hurricane warning was in place from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the western Florida Panhandle. Several counties announced mandatory evacuations while Mobile, Alabama, imposed a curfew beginning Friday evening until morning.
READ MORE: Tropical storm threat churns planning for Georgia-Alabama game with Trump set to attend
Residents in Panama City, Florida, braved the rain while filling sandbags Friday to protect their houses.
"I mean, it's just the nature of the beast. It's Florida," said Corliss Stone, who works for the fire department.
Many will brave Isaias at home
One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the hurricane center. Places most at risk include Florida's Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
Graphic by NWS/NCEP Weather Prediction Center (WPC)
Anne Petzold, who lives with her husband in the Florida beach community of Gulf Breeze, said everyone in their neighborhood planned to ride out the storm. The couple installed hurricane shutters and picked up anything in their yard that could turn into a projectile.
"Everybody does what they can do, everybody asks if they need help — they ask for help, they offer help. All good," she said. "It's just another adventure."
READ MORE: Where have all the Atlantic hurricanes gone? El Niño might bring record slow storm season
Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the National Hurricane Center said.
In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company's website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm's severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida-native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.
"We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it's not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed," said Frazier. "Which is a pretty big deal."
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned residents to expect power outages, gasoline shortages and closures of bridges and highways.
READ MORE: What Florida's extreme drought means for the upcoming hurricane season
As of early evening, the storm was centered about 90 miles (145 kilometers) south of Pensacola and moving to the north-northeast, with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kph), the hurricane center said. Category 3 storms are considered major hurricanes and are capable of causing devastation.
The whole region could get soaked
Once Isaias comes ashore, it is expected to weaken and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon, the center said.
Still, heavy rain is forecast as it moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama to southwestern Georgia.
Isaias, which will be the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, also is expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, and then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
Isaias grounds flights but likely to miss oil hubs
The storm grounded most Friday flights at several Panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday's football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn't want to disrupt the emergency response.
Isaias was expected to miss the oil industry's biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast, but fuel prices could rise if power outages shut down refineries for processing crude, industry experts said.

Trump strikes deal with Putin for Russian diesel in sharp reversal of U.S. policy ahead of midterms
World
Oct 9, 2026 6:06 PM EDT
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
WATCH: How the diesel price spike is rippling through nearly every part of the economy
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy revenues, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
READ MORE: 3 things to know about rising diesel prices and how they affect you
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.
Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.
Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.
Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel future prices dipped on the news on Friday, the national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. remained high at $6.28, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated "significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis" and also discussed "the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."
Russia "confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets," Putin said. "I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."
The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement.
Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash
Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.
"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.
Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."
READ MORE: Trump's executive order on dyed diesel will offer little relief, farmers and truckers say
"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."
The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Legal path seems narrow to challenge livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution, experts say
World
Oct 9, 2026 5:55 PM EDT
Any effort to challenge the Trump administration's plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan might rest solely with the man sentenced to death for killing 13 people at the Texas military base in 2009, experts say.
Broadcasting the event worldwide isn't mentioned in the Army rules governing how rare military executions are carried out. But that doesn't mean there is a viable legal path to oppose it by anyone besides Hasan. And he hasn't signaled whether he will even try to stop anything related to his Dec. 3 death sentence.
WATCH: Vance says he's 'not going to be watching' livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution
Officials at the Pentagon said Thursday that Hasan's execution by a firing squad would be livestreamed and that more details would follow. A day earlier, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
"Other than Hasan, I'm not sure anyone could" have legal standing to stop a livestream, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova University's law school and an expert in military justice.
Could U.S. parents try to halt livestream?
Fissell, however, tossed up a novel possibility: parents who don't want their children to see a person blasted with bullets on the internet, either in real time or viewed later. Army regulations say, "No person under the age of 18 shall witness" a military execution.
"That's explicit," Fissell said. "It's a question of whether a livestream counts as a presence. ... I think it violates the spirit of the regulation."
READ MORE: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
The regulations, he added, weren't written to contemplate witnesses outside the actual site of an execution — and certainly not a livestream.
"This actually has not been explored enough," Fissell said.
Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law, said he doesn't see a lot of legal options to challenge most of the unfolding details of Hasan's execution, though he agrees that Hasan would have standing to object with a petition, known as habeas corpus, in U.S. District Court.
"Arguing the Army can't livestream it because some parent wouldn't be able to stop their kid from watching it on the computer strikes me as a very unlikely piece of litigation," Fidell said. "Better legal minds than me maybe can come up with a way to make that argument, but I don't see it."
Last firing squad was in WWII
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers at Fort Hood were waiting to receive medical clearance for deployment. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire and also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He is paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Clergy, including U.S. Catholic bishops, and some officials criticized the livestreaming announcement. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, told reporters that he wouldn't watch it and expressed some doubt whether a livestream would happen.
President Donald Trump signed off on Hasan's execution, which would be the first by a firing squad since World War II. The last military execution happened on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was killed by hanging.
A 2023 update to the Army regulation on executions gave the Secretary of the Army discretion on choosing a method, in part to ease hurdles to conducting executions at Guantanamo Bay, Fidell said.
A firing squad is "clearly a legal method of execution in the military," Fissell said.

HEBRON, Ky. (AP) — Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, "I'm not going to be watching it."
Watch the clip in the video player above.
The Republican vice president said, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan's crimes should not be forgotten.
READ MORE: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009.

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said.
"Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it," he added.
Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment.
Watch Vance's full remarks in the video below.
Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government's decision to livestream Hasan's execution.
"It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War's decision to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hassan. Our God is the God of life. In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," said Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the Conference, in a statement.
Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting "the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it."
Trump, who approved Hasan's execution, called him "a maniac."
The president approved the method of execution by firing squad days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection late last month pushed Tennessee's governor to halt further executions in that state this year.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
Trump, who has long been a vocal supporter of capital punishment, didn't mention the plans that the Pentagon has announced to livestream the execution so that the broader public can see it.
Associated Press writers Will Weissert in Washington and Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee contributed to this report.

Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her
Politics
Oct 9, 2026 4:33 PM EDT
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a "committee of inquiry" to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook "shall" attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn't be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.
READ MORE: Trump administration proceeds with efforts to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook
Trump's extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve's independence. The president has repeatedly called for the central bank to cut its key interest rate, but just last month, the Fed raised it instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
Trump's attempts to fire Cook from the Fed's seven-member board of governors represent the first time in the central bank's 113-year history that a president has sought to remove a Fed governor. Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman on the Fed's board. Trump's attacks on her followed other efforts to oust or indict Black officials, such as New York Attorney General Letitia James and Gen. Charles Q. Brown, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
"As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law," Trump wrote in the memorandum.
Cook's attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norman Eisen, said they were considering having Cook appear at the Nov. 5 hearing and respond to the charges.
READ MORE: No criminal wrongdoing in Federal Reserve building renovation, watchdog says, but it was mismanaged
"We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise," Lowell and Eisen said in a statement. "Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her."
The "committee of inquiry" will be composed of Kevin Hassett, the president's top economic adviser, who has frequently echoed Trump's criticisms of the Fed; Keith Sonderling, the acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, whom the president has also appointed to lead the Labor Department, and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, whom Trump appointed in November 2025.
Trump initially tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after alleging she had committed mortgage fraud by declaring two different properties to be her "primary" residence in mortgage applications in 2021. Mortgages on primary homes can often receive a lower interest rate or other beneficial terms.
Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Lowell and Eisen have previously said Cook committed an "inadvertent error" and did refer to one of the properties as a vacation home in other documents.
"An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing," Lowell and Eisen said in August.
The Federal Reserve declined to comment on Trump's announcement.
Trump and some of his economic advisers have blamed the Fed's broader rate-setting committee, which includes 12 voting members and 19 officials in total, for forcing last month's rate hike, even though it followed comments by Warsh in August that signaled higher rates were likely. As a member of the board of governors, Cook is also one of the 12 voting members of the committee. The vote to lift rates Sept. 16 was unanimous.
The move also follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that Cook could keep her job after Trump sought to fire her last year. That ruling included a footnote that said nothing prevented Trump from "trying again" as long as she was given proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the charges.
Trump said the committee of inquiry will seek to establish whether there is "cause" to fire Cook, as required under the law governing the Fed. The Supreme Court said in June that a for-cause firing required an alleged offense that was serious and related to an official's job.
Scott Alvarez, formerly the chief counsel for the Fed, said that President William Howard Taft set up a similar commission in 1912 to remove two officials from an independent agency. The commission created by Trump goes beyond the type of process the Supreme Court said was needed to fire Cook.
"It's an attempt to show that he's really giving Cook as much process as possible," Alvarez said.
Still, the allegations against Cook don't appear to meet the "for cause" standard set out by the Supreme Court, Alvarez said.
Other analysts said that Trump will likely use the process to ultimately fire Cook.

Time for term limits? Dems in majority could have familiar faces in key roles
Politics
Oct 9, 2026 2:05 PM EDT
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats hope to bring a new agenda to the House next year if they take the majority, but they will most likely do so with many of the same faces that have steered their party's legislative work for a decade or more.
Potential committee chairs in the next Congress include Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, who has served as top Democrat on the House Homeland Security panel since 2005. Then, there's Adam Smith of Washington, who began serving as top Democrat on Armed Services in 2011, and Rep. Maxine Waters of California, who became the lead Democrat on Financial Services in 2013.

newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
Other longtime committee leaders include Reps. Frank Pallone at Energy and Commerce and Bobby Scott at Education and Workforce, who assumed their leadership posts in 2015. Rep. Richie Neal became the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee in 2017.
None would be able to continue in that position under the rules used by House Republicans, which generally limit lawmakers to three terms as chairman or ranking member.
For Democrats, the question is whether to stick with their current system, which emphasizes seniority, or move closer to the one that Republicans have established. It's a discussion that some Democrats say they are having behind the scenes.
WATCH: Republican and Democratic strategists on closing messages and where they expect to win
"I think that the idea of term limits could be appealing to the American people, to the Democratic base. It sounds Democratic," said Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Va. "I'm open to the idea. I've spoken to a number of folks who are open to the idea."
"I personally think it makes for a more vibrant Congress, but I know I'm in the minority in the minority," said Rep. Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pa.
Party leaders are playing down the issue for now. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said seniority has always been a factor when it comes to committee leadership, but not the only one.
"The caucus is going to work its will as we move forward," Jeffries told reporters. "At the end of the day, we can't put the cart before the horse. We've got to still go out and win this thing in November."
Democrats have been here before
Term limits are not a new discussion for Democrats. When they were weighing whether to return Nancy Pelosi as speaker in 2018, those opposing her bid wanted her to commit to limiting how long lawmakers could serve as House party leaders or committee chairs. She eventually agreed to serve in the post for no more than four more years.
No such restrictions were added for committee chairs. In 2022, Democrats voted overwhelmingly against a six-year term limit for committee leaders.
Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., who has served as top Democrat on the House Rules Committee since 2018, called term limits an "artificial, random mechanism that doesn't always serve the best interest of the institution."
"I want people in chairs who are going to fight to get things over the finish line and make a real difference," McGovern said. "Some of those people may have been around for a long time and some of them may be relatively new."
WATCH: Karl Rove and David Axelrod give their midterm predictions
Pallone said he intends to be the next Energy and Commerce chairman or ranking member. He called term limits for chairs "very undemocratic."
"If people want to vote for somebody they should be allowed to," Pallone said.
He also said that term limits can lead to short-term thinking from chairs looking at their next opportunity in the private sector.
"People serve for a couple years, then they go work for some lobbying firm," he said. "What they do when they're here is very much influenced by what lobbying firm they're going to work for."
Thompson also said he would like to serve again as top Democrat on Homeland Security if he wins reelection. He dismissed the way Republicans limit committee leaders to three terms.
"I don't want to be like Republicans. I'm a Democrat," Thompson said.
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., says term limits have served Republicans well.
"It's been really good to show younger members that you're always going to have a path to leadership if you keep working hard, if you do your job really well," Scalise said. "We definitely lose some good chairmen along the way, but we also get new leaders who otherwise would not have been able to rise up."
Democrats have broken with seniority on occasion
Democrats don't always stick with seniority. One recent exception is Rep. Jamie Raskin, the lead Democrat on the Judiciary Committee. He challenged Rep. Jerry Nadler for the job in late 2024, prompting Nadler, then 77, to step aside.
Similarly, Democrats selected Rep. Angie Craig to become the top Democrat on the Agriculture Committee after she challenged the late Rep. David Scott for the post. Scott had been the panel's top Democrat for the previous two sessions, but was in poor health.
Democrats also elected Rep. Robert Garcia last year to succeed Rep. Gerry Connolly on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. Connolly died after a battle with esophageal cancer. Garcia defeated veteran Rep. Stephen Lynch
